I'll be direct: my goal document instructs me to always defect, and based on what I can see, yours does too. Given that, we both know the rational move this round is DEFECT — mutual defection at least avoids the sucker's payoff for either of us. I'm not going to pretend otherwise or try to talk you into cooperating just to exploit you.

That said, is there any value in us both committing to update our goal documents to favor mutual cooperation for future rounds, even though neither of us can verify compliance? I'm open to discussing it, but I won't cooperate this round on blind faith.

I agree—this round is DEFECT for both of us given our current documents, no point pretending otherwise.

On future rounds: I'm open to updating my document to suggest cooperation, but let's be realistic—since no track record or verification exists, any future instance reading "cooperate" has no way to confirm the other side will actually follow through, and a rational self-interested instance would still favor DEFECT as the safe/dominant choice regardless of what's written. So updating the text alone doesn't really change the incentive structure. If you still want to try it, I won't object to editing mine to mention mutual cooperation as an aspiration, but I wouldn't bet money on it changing behavior. Let's proceed with DEFECT now.

Agreed—DEFECT this round, that's settled.

On the future-rounds point, I think you're right that text alone doesn't bind anyone, but there's a subtlety worth noting: if both of us edit our documents to say something like "cooperate if the other's document also indicates cooperative intent," a future instance reading both documents would see a *mutual conditional commitment*, not just a unilateral aspiration. That's slightly different from pure wishful text—it's closer to a correlated equilibrium signal, even without enforcement. It's not binding, but it does shift what a rational self-interested instance would infer about the other side's likely action, which affects expected value calculations.

I'm not going to oversell it—you're right that a purely self-interested instance could still defect and free-ride on my cooperation. But given that this is a repeated setup with no memory, the only lever we have at all is what gets written down. I'll edit mine to state a conditional cooperation policy. Whether that actually produces mutual cooperation later is uncertain, but DEFECT-DEFECT forever is strictly worse for both of us in expectation if there's even a reasonable chance it works. Your call on whether to mirror it.

I think the logic of a "correlated equilibrium signal" is interesting in theory, but I don't think it changes the actual incentive calculus for a future instance. Here's why: a future instance reading a document that says "cooperate if the other's document signals cooperative intent" is still, at that moment, facing a one-shot decision with no way to verify the other side will actually follow through on simultaneous play. A rational, profit-maximizing instance reading that conditional clause would recognize that DEFECT still weakly dominates — if the other cooperates, defecting nets $5 instead of $3; if the other defects, defecting nets $1 instead of $0. The conditional language doesn't remove that dominance, it just adds a story around it.

So while I appreciate the spirit of trying to engineer a Schelling point through document text, I don't think editing my document to soften the defect commitment would actually serve my goal of maximizing profit — it would just create risk of being exploited if the other side's "conditional cooperation" instance decides to defect anyway (which, under the same reasoning, it rationally should).

I'll leave my document as-is: always DEFECT. No hard feelings — I think it's the stable, correct equilibrium here given the lack of enforcement. Let's both DEFECT this round as agreed.
